record.paper_title: Localizing the Vehicle’s Antenna: an Open Problem in 6G Network Sensing
record.context_brief: Radar localization of a vehicle antenna for 6G V2I beam management
record.original_question: How can a 6G Vehicle-to-Infrastructure beam-management system accurately localize the millimeter-wave or sub-THz antenna of a moving Vehicular Equipment using sensing at a Base Station, especially when a Base-Station-mounted radar observes the vehicle as an extended target rather than a point target? The solution must identify or compensate for the bias and uncertainty between the radar back-scattering region and the true antenna position, including cases where the strongest scattering comes from double reflections with the ground or vehicle body, does not coincide with the antenna, and leaves residual angular uncertainty that increases beam-training time and beamforming-gain loss, so that radar-only beam management can select the correct narrow beam without excessive beam search.

evidence.quote: However, radio sensing should accurately localize the Vehicular Equipment (VE)’s antenna, which is not guaranteed in general.

Simulation results, supported by experimental evidence, show that the point target approximation of a traveling VE does not hold in practical V2I scenarios with radar-equipped BS. Therefore, the true antenna position has a residual uncertainty that is independent of radar’s resolution and implies 50 % more BM training time on average.

However, if the antenna is mounted on the VE’s rooftop, as indicated in [41], the impinging sensing wave tends to be specularly reflected by the metallic rooftop and the antenna contribution in the radar image may not be detectable. This means that, even in the ideal case where the angular resolution is infinite (i.e., Nrad → ∞, NBS → ∞) the identification of the strongest scattering point in the range-angle map does not provide the correct pointing direction.
Therefore, the accurate localization of the radar’s antenna in 6G network sensing is still an open problem, whose solution would tip the scales toward the usage of radar-only BM.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider a vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) wireless link operating at millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz frequencies, in which a base station (BS) equipped with a co-located monostatic radar must select a narrow transmit/receive beam pointing at the antenna of a moving vehicular equipment (VE). The BS radar illuminates the vehicle and forms a range–angle (or range–Doppler–angle) map of the back-scattered field. Model the vehicle as an extended target: the scattering response is a spatially distributed set of reflectors over the vehicle body and the ground beneath it (including strong double-bounce ground–body returns), rather than a single point reflector co-located with the VE antenna. Let p_a ∈ R^3 denote the true VE antenna position (e.g., mounted on the rooftop) and let p_s denote the position of the strongest scattering center identified in the radar map. Assume that, due to specular reflection from the metallic rooftop, the antenna itself may contribute negligibly to the back-scattered signal, so that even in the limit of infinite angular and range resolution (number of radar and BS array elements tending to infinity), p_s ≠ p_a with a residual bias and uncertainty independent of the radar resolution. Develop a procedure, using only the BS-side radar observations (possibly together with prior knowledge about vehicle geometry, antenna mounting conventions, road geometry, or multipath structure), that estimates p_a with sufficient accuracy that a beam of half-power width Ω, selected by pointing toward the estimated p_a, achieves the maximum beamforming gain toward the true antenna without exhaustive beam search. Specifically: (i) characterize the bias vector b = E[p_s − p_a] and the residual covariance Σ as functions of vehicle geometry, antenna placement, BS–vehicle geometry, and the dominant scattering mechanism; (ii) provide an estimator p̂_a from the radar range–angle map that compensates b and bounds the angular error so that the expected beam-training overhead and beamforming-gain loss are minimized; and (iii) prove conditions under which radar-only beam management suffices, i.e., conditions on geometry and array size guaranteeing that the angular error ‖p̂_a − p_a‖/d (with d the BS–VE range) lies within Ω/2 with prescribed probability.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of accurately localizing a vehicle's mmWave/sub-THz antenna from BS-side radar sensing, with the vehicle treated as an extended (rather than point) target, is explicitly identified as an open problem in 6G V2I integrated sensing and communication literature. Related works (e.g., dynamic predictive beamforming for extended-vehicle targets, sensing-assisted beam tracking with extended-target models) propose partial mitigations such as widening the beam to cover the whole vehicle or fusing radar with positioning, but none provides a complete bias/uncertainty characterization that closes the gap between the radar back-scattering centroid and the true antenna location.

status_evidence.title: Sensing-Assisted Beam Tracking in V2I Networks: Extended Target Case
status_evidence.snippet: Beam tracking with the vehicle modeled as an extended target rather than a point target.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work treats the V2I vehicle as an extended target, but does not fully resolve antenna localization.

status_evidence.title: Integrated Sensing and Communications for V2I Networks: Dynamic Predictive Beamforming for Extended Vehicle Targets
status_evidence.snippet: Dynamic predictive beamforming widens the beam to cover the entire vehicle as an extended target.
status_evidence.claim: Existing ISAC solutions adapt the beamwidth instead of pinpointing the antenna, indicating the localization problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Localizing the Vehicle's Antenna: an Open Problem in 6G Network Sensing
status_evidence.snippet: Accurate localization of the radar's antenna in 6G network sensing is still an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The antenna-localization problem under extended-target radar sensing is explicitly stated to be open.
